item.title: Laboratory evaluation of FINER completed
item.description: The integrated test of the full FINER system at NAOJ, including the warm optics, both front-end receivers, the local oscillators, the IF chain and the DRS4 spectrometers, has been completed. FINER is now being prepared for its journey to the LMT in Mexico.

item.title: FINER papers presented at SPIE Astronomical Telescopes + Instrumentation 2026
item.description: Two new papers on FINER are available on arXiv: the system development and preparations for first light (Taniguchi et al. 2026) and the 210–350 GHz wideband receiver (Kang et al. 2026).

item.title: The FINER "periscope" is ready
item.description: The warm optics of FINER, a coupling optical mechanism that picks up the radio waves collected by the LMT and leads them to the FINER receiver, is ready. Tatsuya Takekoshi at Kitami Institute of Technology is finalizing its integration.

item.title: FINER receiver used for a dark photon search (DOSUE-RR)
item.description: Before its shipment to the LMT, the FINER Band 6+7 receiver (210–350 GHz) is being used at NAOJ by DOSUE-RR, an experiment that searches for dark matter with radio waves. The team led by Okayama University, including Associate Professor Adachi, installed its own calibration and readout system on FINER and started the search for dark photons in the 0.9–1.4 meV mass range on 6 April 2026. See the announcement by Okayama University (in Japanese).

item.title: We released the LMT/B4R Commissioning Report in 2024
item.description:
We have released the LMT/B4R Commissioning and Science Observations Report in 2024. B4R is a 2-mm dual-polarization 2SB heterodyne receiver system (Kawabe et al. 2025, AJ, 170, 350; Yonetsu et al. 2025, arXiv:2511.21845) and the precursor of the FINER receiver system.

  • Link to the report (Google Drive)

item.title: Laboratory evaluation of FINER has started at NAOJ
item.description: The laboratory evaluation of the FINER receiver has started at NAOJ in preparation for installation on the LMT. Masato Hagimoto and graduate student Kato are leading the measurements.

item.title: FINER collaboration meeting at ASIAA
item.description: The FINER team held a collaboration meeting at the Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics (ASIAA) in Taipei.

item.title: FINER papers presented at SPIE Astronomical Telescopes + Instrumentation 2024
item.description:
A series of papers on FINER is now available on arXiv and was presented at SPIE Astronomical Telescopes + Instrumentation 2024 in Yokohama. Haoran Kang and Masato Hagimoto reported the development status of the receiver and the spectrometer.

  • Tamura et al. 2024: project overview
  • Kang et al. 2024: receivers
  • Hagimoto et al. 2024: digital spectrometer array

item.title: FINER meeting at INAOE and observations at the LMT
item.description: Members of the FINER team visited the LMT office at INAOE in Puebla, Mexico, and discussed the FINER receiver with the LMT team. The team then went up to the summit of Sierra Negra (4,600 m) for receiver tests and observations of molecular gas in distant galaxies.

item.title: FINER project has started with ALMA2 receiver technology
item.description: The FINER project has entered its development phase. This week we signed a research agreement with the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ), under which FINER will use the receiver technologies developed for ALMA2, the next-generation upgrade of ALMA. Together with the Large Millimeter Telescope in Mexico, FINER aims at the highest spectral-scanning sensitivity in the northern hemisphere to identify distant galaxies that remain unidentified in the northern sky.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How can I use FINER?

FINER will be offered on the LMT through the regular LMT Call for Proposals after commissioning. Observing time on the LMT is allocated to the LMT partner communities, and eligibility to propose follows the rules of each Call; there is currently no formal route for proposers outside the LMT partnership.

When does FINER come online?

FINER is expected to come online in 2027, after installation and commissioning on the LMT.

Can I join FINER development?

Yes. We welcome new collaborators in the development of FINER. Please contact the PI, Yoichi Tamura (Nagoya University; ytamura (at) nagoya-u.jp).

item.title: Receiver
item.description:
Specifications

FINER is a dual-polarization, sideband-separating (2SB) SIS receiver system. The table below summarizes the configuration installed for first light and the design goals of the full system.

General
Number of bands 2 (one band observed at a time at first light)
Number of beams per band 1
Number of polarizations per band 2
Number of sidebands per band 2 (2SB)
Band 4 (first light) Band 6+7 Band 4+5 (planned upgrade)
Radio frequency ≈138–178 GHz ≈210–351 GHz 120–210 GHz
Intermediate frequency (per sideband, per polarization) 4–8 GHz 4–20 GHz 4–20 GHz
Receiver noise temperature (SSB, design goal) — 75 K 45 K

Measured performance will be reported here after commissioning on the LMT.

System overview

At first light FINER has two front-end receivers in a single cryostat: a Band 4 MMIC receiver and a wideband Band 6+7 receiver, both developed at NAOJ. A wideband Band 4+5 receiver covering 120–210 GHz is planned as a later upgrade. IF switches select which band feeds the four IF chains, so one band is observed at a time; simultaneous dual-band observation is an option for a future optics upgrade.

Figure. Block diagram of the full FINER system (design).

Optics

The FINER warm optics picks off the beam after the LMT’s M4 mirror with a pair of motorized mirrors (the “periscope”), which can be set and stowed remotely. A chopper with a blackbody load is used for intensity calibration. A fast sky chopper for quick position switching is planned in a later phase. The spatial resolution (PSF size) is about 7 arcsec × (frequency / 200 GHz)−1.

Front-end receivers

The front-end receivers exploit the high critical current density SIS mixer technology developed for the ALMA Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU) (Kojima et al. 2017, 2020; Kang et al. 2026), which provides a wide instantaneous frequency coverage.

Back-end spectrometers

  • Wideband spectrometers (DRS4, ELECS Inc.). Two DRS4 chassis digitize eight 10.24 GHz-wide basebands with 3-bit, 20.48 GSa/s analog-to-digital converters and provide spectra with 20 MHz resolution (Hagimoto et al. 2024). Sideband separation is also performed digitally.
  • High-resolution spectrometers (XFFTS, RPG). The XFFTS spectrometers of the LMT 2-mm receiver B4R (2.5 GHz bandwidth, 88 kHz resolution) remain available for high-resolution spectroscopy.

Data and software

FINER is controlled from the LMT Telescope Control System. The data format and the reduction pipeline are being developed together with the LMT team.

item.title: Science
item.description:
Galaxy formation

Background: Galaxy formation in the epoch of reionization and beyond

How and when the first galaxies form in the earliest Universe is one of the most fundamental questions in modern astronomy. The pristine materials in the early universe cooled down to form neutral hydrogen at redshift z ~ 1000 or 380k years after the Big Bang. Once first stars and galaxies are born, however, the hydrogen gas in the intergalactic space is ʻreionizedʼ by hydrogen-ionizing photons from the hot, massive stars. This so-called cosmic reionization is indirect evidence for the birth of the first luminous objects. In recent years, Planck satellite has reported that cosmic reionization occurred in the period centered at redshift z = 7.8 (660 million years after the Big Bang, Planck Collaboration 2018), whereas more than 100 galaxy candidates have been identified with Hubble even before the period (e.g., Bouwens et al. 2018, see recent achievements with JWST), meaning that we are likely witnessing the birth of the earliest galaxies in the universe.

In particular, finding massive galaxies in the era is difficult but is expected to offer unique information on galaxy formation, because the probability of finding them (i.e., volume density or luminosity function) depends on cosmic structure formation models. Then, the key questions we are trying to address in this research are

  • when massive galaxies emerge,
  • how common they are in the pre-reionization era,
  • what controls their growth.

It is, however, difficult to confirm galaxy “candidates” in the era; in general, identifying an object as a galaxy and determining its physical properties begin with spectroscopy of atomic or molecular spectral lines. But the combination of bright spectral lines and a sensitive instrument that are sufficient for detection of a galaxy even in the furthest universe is very limited.

Key science goals

In this study, we aim for a sensitive spectroscopic survey of galaxies in the pre-reionization era using the far-infrared fine-structure lines, [O III] 88 μm and [C II] 158 μm, that are demonstrated to be bright (Inoue et al. 2016), based on our novel millimeter and submillimeter-wave receiver, FINER, for Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT). We also aim to elucidate their physical properties.

How FINER helps?

FINER offers an instantaneous bandwidth 5 times wider than ALMA, while achieving the same sensitivity as ALMA. LMT-FINER will provide 40% of ALMAʼs light-collecting area, a similar atmospheric transmittance to ALMA, and a 5 times wider bandwidth than ALMA. This offers the most sensitive spectral-scanning capability among millimeter and submillimeter telescopes in the northern hemisphere.

Further cases

On top of that, FINER also offers a unique capability for broader science cases as follows.

  • Solar system
  • Interstellar medium
  • Star formation
  • Nearby galaxies
  • Distant submillimeter-bright galaxies
